subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the approximate radius of an atom?
questions.explain: Atoms have a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, while the nucleus is around 10 000 times smaller.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, with electrons orbiting around it.

questions.q: What are the relative charges of a proton, a neutron and an electron?
questions.explain: A proton has relative charge +1, a neutron 0 and an electron −1.

questions.q: What best describes isotopes of an element?
options: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
Atoms with different numbers of protons and electrons
Atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers
questions.explain: Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers.

questions.q: The mass number of an atom tells you the total number of which particles?
questions.explain: The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.q: The alpha particle scattering experiment led scientists to replace the plum pudding model with which model?
options: The Bohr shell model with fixed energies
questions.explain: Alpha scattering showed mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, giving the nuclear model.

questions.q: In the alpha scattering experiment, what did most of the alpha particles do?
options: Passed straight through the gold foil
questions.explain: Most alpha particles passed straight through, showing the atom is mostly empty space.

questions.q: What happens when an electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation?
options: It moves to a higher energy level further from the nucleus
It moves to a lower energy level closer to the nucleus
It is emitted from the atom as a beta particle
questions.explain: Absorbing EM radiation raises an electron to a higher energy level; emitting radiation returns it to a lower level.

questions.q: In which unit is the activity of a radioactive source measured?
questions.explain: Activity is the rate of decay, measured in becquerel, where 1 Bq is one decay per second.

questions.q: What is an alpha particle?
options: Two neutrons and two protons (a helium nucleus)
A high-speed electron from the nucleus
questions.explain: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus consisting of two protons and two neutrons.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is the most ionising but the least penetrating?
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is strongly ionising but is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: A beta particle is best described as which of the following?
options: A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
A proton emitted from the nucleus
questions.explain: A beta particle is a fast electron emitted when a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton.

questions.q: Which material is needed to stop beta radiation?
questions.explain: Beta radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; paper stops alpha and thick lead is needed for gamma.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, how do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2
Mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1
Mass number decreases by 2 and atomic number decreases by 4
Mass number and atomic number both stay the same
questions.explain: Losing an alpha particle (2 protons, 2 neutrons) reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a beta particle, how do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1
Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2
Mass number increases by 1 and atomic number stays the same
Mass number and atomic number both decrease by 1
questions.explain: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton, so the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by 1.

questions.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 18 hours?
questions.explain: 18 hours is three half-lives, so the number of nuclei halves three times: 1 → 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8.

questions.q: An atom is written as ⁿ₁₁Na with mass number 23. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12.

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source; contamination is having radioactive atoms on or in an object
Contamination is exposure to radiation from an outside source; irradiation is having radioactive atoms on or in an object
Both mean the object becomes radioactive permanently
Both mean the object is exposed only to gamma rays
questions.explain: Irradiation does not make an object radioactive, whereas contamination places radioactive atoms on or inside it.

questions.q: Which of these is commonly used as the fuel that undergoes nuclear fission?
questions.explain: Nuclear fission typically uses large unstable nuclei such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239.

questions.q: What is nuclear fusion?
options: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy
A nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes stable
An electron and a proton combine to form a neutron
questions.explain: In fusion two light nuclei join to make a heavier nucleus, with some mass converted into energy, as happens in stars.
